sections.html: Corydoras nijsseni is the smallest and cutest of all the different "orange blotch" Corydoras from the Rio Negro. This fish is a close relative of C. elegans.

The orange-blotch coloration, which is the same in Corydoras adolfoi, C. duplicareus, C. imitator, C. sp. C39, C. serratus, and several other species, does not reflect the phylogenetic relationship at all. Research has shown that it is simply a case of mimicry that is used as a protection against predators. A bird or another fish-eating animal will learn from the first Corydoras it preys on that they are nasty scratchy in the throat. In future it will avoid feeding on such fish. So all fish with the same coloration are protected; this is the sense of this mimicry.

As in most members of the Corydoras elegans group (the generic name Gastrodermus is available for them), males and females show quite different coloration. Males are much darker during the mating season. Very old males can even develop a black-dark network all over the body. However, the fish imported are still young adults and the difference is therefore not yet clearly visible.
